prompt: What does exploratory testing mean, in the definition most teams quote?
hint: Three activities, and when they happen.

choices.text: Testing without any plan, when no test cases were written
choices.why: That is the reputation; the definition is about doing three things at once.

choices.text: Learning, test design and test execution at the same time
choices.why: Right: each result decides the next test.

choices.text: Running scripted cases in a random order to find hidden dependencies
choices.why: The cases are still designed in advance, so it is scripted testing.

choices.text: Testing done by users rather than by testers
choices.why: That is closer to acceptance testing, lesson 12.

prompt: Ana sees an odd message and tries the same action from another state. What makes that exploratory rather than scripted?
hint: Where did the second test come from?

choices.text: She used curl instead of the browser
choices.why: The tool does not decide it; a script can use curl too.

choices.text: Nobody will ever be able to repeat what she did
choices.why: Her notes make it repeatable; that is not the difference.

choices.text: The first answer decided the second test
choices.why: Right: the design happened during the run, not before it.

choices.text: The action she tried is not listed in the requirements of the application
choices.why: Pay, use and cancel are all in R6.

prompt: Every scripted case for the order page passes, and the counter staff still complain about it. What does this lesson suggest?
hint: Four places where exploration pays most.

choices.text: An exploratory session on the order page
choices.why: Right: passing scripts and live complaints mean the questions nobody wrote.

choices.text: Running the same scripted cases again, more carefully
choices.why: They already pass; running them again asks the same questions.

choices.text: Closing the complaints, since the cases prove the page works
choices.why: The cases prove what they check, and the complaints are about something else.

choices.text: A smoke test of the order page on every build
choices.why: Smoke checks that it comes up; the complaints are about how it behaves.

prompt: What makes exploration plannable and reportable in session-based test management?
hint: What does each session leave behind?

choices.text: Every session is turned into a full set of scripted cases before it runs
choices.why: Then it would be scripted testing.

choices.text: A tool records every click the tester makes
choices.why: No tool is needed; a sheet and a conversation are.

choices.text: Only senior testers are allowed to explore
choices.why: Nothing in the method depends on seniority.

choices.text: Sessions with a charter and a sheet, counted per area
choices.why: Right: a manager counts sessions per area the way cases are counted.

prompt: Hendrickson's charter template reads: Explore a target, with resources, to ___ information.
hint: The part that says when the session has done its job.

prompt: Which of these is a test case wearing a charter's words?
hint: One expected result, nothing to discover.

choices.text: Explore sign-up with names at and beyond R2's limits, to discover how odd input is treated
choices.why: A target, resources and a question: a well-formed charter.

choices.text: Explore booking to check that six tickets are accepted
choices.why: Right: one check with one expected result; it belongs in a suite.

choices.text: Explore boxoffice
choices.why: That is the other mistake: too wide, with no question at all.

choices.text: Explore the seat count with many small orders, to discover whether the page matches sales
choices.why: A target, resources and a question: a well-formed charter.

prompt: Which part of a charter is most often left out, and most worth writing?
hint: It says when the session is done.

choices.text: The target
choices.why: Nobody forgets what they are exploring; they forget why.

choices.text: The resources
choices.why: Useful, and still not what tells you the session has done its job.

choices.text: The information to discover
choices.why: Right: the question is what tells you when the session has done its job.

choices.text: The tester's name
choices.why: The sheet carries it; the charter is about the mission.

prompt: Half an hour into a session on orders, Ana notices that the Shows page seems to show the wrong seat count. What does the method say she does?
hint: The charter is a direction.

choices.text: Ignores it: anything outside the charter is out of scope for the session
choices.why: The charter is a direction, not a fence; a finding is never thrown away.

choices.text: Stops the session and starts a new one on seats
choices.why: She may follow it, but the decision comes after writing it down.

choices.text: Files a defect at once, before checking anything else
choices.why: She has not yet confirmed it; a note comes first.

choices.text: Notes it as an opportunity, then decides whether to follow it now
choices.why: Right: and the sheet shows how much time went to it.

prompt: Match each SFDPOT word to the boxoffice question it suggests.
hint: Six things a product is; four of them here.

pairs.right: Which pages exist that no link leads to?
What happens to an order number that does not exist?
What changes once a show has started?

prompt: What is a heuristic, as this lesson uses the word?
hint: It does not promise anything.

choices.text: A checklist that must be completed before a session can end
choices.why: It is a question generator, not a list to finish.

choices.text: A fallible rule of thumb for coming up with a test
choices.why: Right: it suggests a question and promises no defect.

choices.text: A talent for finding defects that some testers are born with
choices.why: That is the picture the section corrects; heuristics can be lent.

choices.text: A formal technique like boundary values, with a correct answer
choices.why: Lesson 4's techniques derive cases; a heuristic only prompts ideas.

prompt: On boxoffice, which visit is Whittaker's back alley tour?
hint: The features hardly anybody uses.

choices.text: Booking a show and paying for it, end to end
choices.why: That is the money tour: what customers pay for.

choices.text: Sign up, book and pay, then the same in another order
choices.why: That is the landmark tour: the main features in different orders.

choices.text: The outbox, /health, an order page opened by its number
choices.why: Right: hardly used, so hardly tested either.

choices.text: Booking 0, 7 and 6 tickets
choices.why: That is Goldilocks, a heuristic for data.

prompt: No customer can press a button called dance. Why was sending action=dance with curl still worth Ana's minute?
hint: What does danceed prove about the message?

choices.text: It is a third defect, and customers will meet it
choices.why: The browser offers four buttons; nobody meets it, which is why it is evidence and not a report.

choices.text: It shows the sentence is assembled from whatever word arrives
choices.why: Right: it tells Rui where to look and why every refusal is affected.

choices.text: It checks that the server rejects attacks
choices.why: The point was the message, not security; and the server answered normally.

choices.text: R6 lists dance as an action to be refused
choices.why: R6 lists four actions; dance is not one.

prompt: Why does Ana cancel a fresh order and then try to pay it, after seeing useed and payed?
hint: She wants a word the application spells itself.

choices.text: To get the seats back before the next test
choices.why: Seats are not the subject of the note she is checking.

choices.text: R6 says cancelled orders can be paid
choices.why: R6 says only a reserved order can be paid.

choices.text: To set a state name the app writes out beside a built action word
choices.why: Right: cancelled with two l's beside payed shows how the message is made.

choices.text: To repeat the first test exactly, as a retest
choices.why: It is a new test chosen from the first result.

prompt: With BOXOFFICE_NOW at 20:30, why can Ana not test a refund after The Seagull has started?
hint: Where would the order come from?

choices.text: The variable is ignored for refunds
choices.why: The clock applies to everything; the problem is the order.

choices.text: A restart empties orders, and booking closed at 19:00
choices.why: Right: a fixed clock cannot move with an order in hand.

choices.text: Refunds are only possible with curl, not in the browser
choices.why: Refund is a button on the order page.

choices.text: The Seagull is not on the calendar when the clock is set by hand
choices.why: The shows are placed around whatever date the clock says.

prompt: Counting the four states an order can reach after it is reserved, plus reserved itself, and R6's four actions, how many action and state pairs does "every action from every state" mean?
hint: States times actions.

prompt: In the session, the refund of a used order is accepted. Why does Ana write "known, seen again" instead of a defect?
hint: Lesson 10 named this case.

choices.text: Exploratory sessions never produce defect reports
choices.why: This one produces two.

choices.text: R6 allows a used order to be refunded
choices.why: It does not; that is why it is a defect at all.

choices.text: Lesson 5 reported it and it is still open
choices.why: Right: a known failure is recorded, not reported twice.

choices.text: It is off-charter, so it is left for another session
choices.why: Order states are exactly her charter.

prompt: Put the PROOF questions of a debrief in order.
hint: The word spells the order.
items: Obstacles: what got in the way?
Feelings: how does the tester feel about the area?
trap: Feelings first would colour the rest before anybody had heard what happened.

prompt: The clock that cannot move with orders in hand: how does the debrief treat it?
hint: Is the application wrong, or hard to test?

choices.text: As a defect against R6, since refunds are involved
choices.why: R6 is met or not by the refund itself; the clock is about testing it.

choices.text: As a testability request to Rui
choices.why: Right: a way to move the clock would turn an hour into a minute.

choices.text: As a reason to drop time from future charters
choices.why: It is the letter most sessions skip already.

choices.text: It is not mentioned, since it was solved in the evening
choices.why: Solving it cost an hour; that is exactly what an obstacle is.

prompt: Ana says the order area feels shakier than its scripted cases suggested. What does that change, by lesson 1's rules?
hint: Every defect is evidence about something.

choices.text: Nothing: a feeling is not evidence and stays out of the plan
choices.why: Here it rests on three defects in one area, which is evidence.

choices.text: The scripted cases for orders are deleted, since they missed the defects
choices.why: They still check what they check; the area just needs more.

choices.text: Risk C's likelihood goes up, so it moves up the ranking
choices.why: Right: a part that keeps failing moves up.

choices.text: The impact of a wrong refund goes up
choices.why: Impact is the harm, which the business judges; the defects speak to likelihood.

prompt: Which of these does a session and its debrief leave behind? Choose every one that does.
hint: Look at the table at the end of section 06.

choices.text: Defect reports
choices.why: Right: two, from Ana's session.

choices.text: Cases for the regression suite
choices.why: Right: one per defect, so the fixes are kept.

choices.text: New charters
choices.why: Right: the outlook becomes the next session.

choices.text: A verdict that the release can ship
choices.why: A session answers its charter; the release decision uses much more.

choices.text: A replacement for the scripted suite of the area
choices.why: Exploration finds what scripts miss; it does not replace them.

prompt: Boxoffice 1.2 adds gift vouchers that can pay part of an order. Which charter fits a first session on them?
hint: Target, resources, information; a session's worth.

choices.text: Explore boxoffice 1.2 to find defects
choices.why: Too wide: no target narrower than the product, no question.

choices.text: Check that a voucher of R$ 50,00 takes R$ 50,00 off
choices.why: Too narrow: one expected result is a test case.

choices.text: Explore paying with vouchers, with discounts and refunds, to discover how they combine
choices.why: Right: a target, resources and a question nobody has an answer to yet.

choices.text: Run every scripted case of 1.1 again, then look at vouchers
choices.why: That is a regression run with exploration left for the end.
